newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Foreign executives sour on Asia but Manila shines.
newsitem.headline: Foreign executives sour on Asia but Manila shines.

text.p: Expatriate executives were more critical of Asia's shortcomings this year than in the recent past, with corruption and red tape high on the list of complaints, a report said on Tuesday.
Exceptions to the gloomy picture were the Philippines, where President Fidel Ramos was seen making progress against endemic problems, and Singapore, whose pro-business environment earned high marks.

The Hong Kong-based Political and Economic Risk Consultancy Ltd (PERC) said in its annual comparative country risk report that South Korea's bureaucracy, expensive labour market and high interest rates drew a large number of complaints.

"Expatriate businessmen in Asia are, in general, more critical of Asia this year. This could be because the economies of most Asian countries have slowed, making businessmen more conscious of the region's socio-political shortcomings," it said.
As far as corruption is concerned, Indonesia was the country where the problem was "considered to be the most severe".
"Illegal levies and under-the-table payments abound, adding greatly to total business costs," the report added.
Not far behind Indonesia in corruption were China and India, where it was seen as a formidable problem.
The problem was also rated as serious in Vietnam.
"The authorities will have to do a lot more than launch periodic clean-up drives against high-level targets if the present scope of corruption is to be reduced," the report said.
PERC praised the progress made by the Philippines, although it said problems in the use of the legal system to block commercial deals rankled.
"The Philippines stood out as the one country where foreign businessmen are decidedly more optimistic," PERC said.
President Fidel Ramos was seen making headway in eliminating a range of socio-political problems like corruption, bureaucracy and discriminatory policies against foreign companies.
"Problems remain, but the country definitely seems to be headed in the right direction," the report concluded.
On Singapore, it said bureaucracy was not a problem and the civil service was known across the region for its efficiency and honesty.
"Business may not always like the policies and regulations which are carried out with such dedication by the civil service, but they are left in no doubt as to where they stand," the PERC said.
